Question six. Define expectation and variance. Expectation is the probability-weighted average. For a fair die, it's three and a half: the point where the faces balance, though no face shows it. Variance is the expected squared distance from that mean: six and a quarter for a one or a six, a quarter for a three or a four. Averaged, about two point nine two. Question seven. What is linearity of expectation, and why is it so useful? The expectation of a sum is the sum of the expectations, even when the parts depend on each other. So split a hard count into easy pieces. Ten people get their hats back at random. Each has a one in ten chance of getting their own, so on average, exactly one does. A hundred thousand shuffles agree. Variance only adds up like that when the parts are uncorrelated. Now the shapes you'll be asked to name.

Question eight. Walk through the distributions a data scientist should know. A Bernoulli is one yes or no trial. A binomial counts the successes in n of them, with mean n times p. A Poisson counts events in an interval, and its mean and variance are both its rate, lambda. The normal is the symmetric bell, with sixty-eight, ninety-five and ninety-nine point seven percent of values within one, two and three standard deviations of the mean. And the exponential is the wait between Poisson events.

Question nine. What does memoryless mean for the exponential? Time already spent waiting changes nothing about the time still to come. Say waits average twelve minutes. The chance of waiting ten more is forty-three percent, whether you've waited zero minutes, ten, or thirty. No other continuous distribution does that.
